stage_a.note: Strong, engaging delivery with clear positive energy throughout the pitch.
High energy, strong voice, and clear engagement with the product and its benefits.
Friendly, approachable demeanor, smiling and making good eye contact with the panel.

venture.description: A portable adapter that turns standard dumbbells into kettlebells.
venture.note: The founders ask for $300,000 for 10% equity.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Dan and Andy present Kettle Gryp, a portable adapter that turns standard dumbbells into kettlebells, asking for 300k for 10 percent.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Robert walks up to the display and talks through the steps of putting a dumbbell into the adapter.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Robert jokes that the founders gave him a heavy dumbbell to use for the demonstration.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Mark lifts the product and remarks on its straightforward use.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Daymond compliments Mark on his lifting form.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Lori asks Kevin how heavy the dumbbell he is holding is.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Kevin demonstrates lifting the product for Lori.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Mark praises the product as a very clever idea.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Robert tells the founders that using the adapter actually feels better than using a standard kettlebell.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Dan agrees with Robert, explaining that standard kettlebells can crunch the user's hands while their grip is comfortable.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Mark asks for the maximum weight of the dumbbell that the adapter can safely hold.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Dan answers that the adapter is currently rated to hold a dumbbell of up to 55 pounds.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Robert expresses positive surprise that it can hold 55 pounds without any problems.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Kevin questions the three million dollar valuation, stating they need a lot of sales to justify it.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Dan confirms they have sales, stating their lifetime sales amount to 3.6 million dollars.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Daymond expresses being impressed and asks to hear the sales figures broken down by year.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Dan states that in 2018 they sold 391,000 dollars worth of product.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Kevin asks for the sales figure for 2019.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Dan states their 2019 sales were 590,000 dollars.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Robert expresses surprise and asks for the 2020 sales figure.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Dan explains that when gyms closed due to Covid, demand skyrocketed, leading to 1.9 million dollars in 2020 sales.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Robert asks what their sales are for the current year of 2021.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Dan answers they have sold 680,000 dollars year to date and project finishing the year at one million.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Daymond asks Dan if his background is in sales or if he is acting as a spokesperson.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Dan replies he was never in sales, having served as a Marine Corps helicopter pilot for twenty years.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Daymond and Robert thank Dan for his military service.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Robert asks Dan what kind of helicopters he flew during his service.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Dan explains he flew the Cobra attack helicopter on multiple deployments to Iraq and Afghanistan.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Robert calls Dan a badass for his military background.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Dan humbly replies he was just doing his job and praises the helicopter he flew.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Robert asks Andy to explain his own professional background.

turns.speaker: F2
turns.summary: Andy explains they have been friends since high school and he previously owned multiple ice cream stores.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Robert asks what the product costs to manufacture and what its retail selling price is.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Dan states the product costs 6.57 dollars to make and sells for 34.95 dollars.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Lori notes that this represents an 81 percent profit margin.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Dan and Andy explain that consumers save money and space by buying their product instead of a full kettlebell set.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Robert asks if they are manufacturing the product themselves.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Dan answers that the product is one hundred percent made in the USA.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Kevin claps and praises them for manufacturing domestically.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Lori asks if they have a patent on the product.

turns.speaker: F2
turns.summary: Andy confirms they have a utility patent that protects the way the closure integrates into the handle.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Mark asks how many knockoff products they have seen in their four years of business.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Dan answers there are about two or three knockoffs, but they are not nearly as successful.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Mark asks what price point the competing knockoff products are selling at.

turns.speaker: F2
turns.summary: Andy explains the knockoffs are cheaper but are of lower quality and not nearly as safe.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Mark asks why they are seeking investment given their high sales and strong profit margins.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Dan explains they need a strategic partner to help them make connections to get into big box retail stores.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Mark asks why retail buyers are not returning their calls or agreeing to stock the product.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Dan admits they are not marketers and have focused their skills on production instead.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Daymond suggests their high sales figures indicate they might be better marketers than they realize.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Robert asks for clarification on what Daymond means by selling a million dollars one unit at a time.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Dan clarifies the unit volume, stating they have sold exactly 106,003 units over the lifetime of the business.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Dan jokes that they just keep selling the units, prompting laughter from the panel.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Mark plays along, jokingly asking what the updated sales number is now.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Dan jokes back that the number has already increased to 106,005 units.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Robert praises the founders but exits because he does not see how the business can grow beyond its current state.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Dan humorously compliments Robert's hair in response to his exit.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Mark exits, citing concerns that the product's reliance on consumers already owning dumbbells limits its market size.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Dan jokes that they will take Mark back if he changes his mind later.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Kevin asks if the founders are familiar with his previous investment in the PRX gym equipment company.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Dan confirms they have seen Kevin's deal in that space.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Kevin offers 300,000 dollars for 20 percent equity, citing his ability to get them into retail through his PRX connections.

turns.speaker: F2
turns.summary: Andy calls Kevin's offer interesting but asks to hear from the other investors out of respect.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Kevin agrees and asks Daymond and Lori what they want to do.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Daymond points out that Lori has been quiet during the discussion.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Lori praises their sales but expresses hesitation about whether she wants to be in the conversion business.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Lori offers 300,000 dollars for 20 percent as preferred stock, so she gets paid distributions first.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Dan counters Lori's offer, asking if she would be willing to drop the equity to 15 percent.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Lori immediately accepts Dan's counter offer.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Dan confirms the deal and the founders celebrate.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Mark congratulates the founders on securing the deal with Lori.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Daymond remarks that he should have jumped in quicker but they will never know what he would have offered.

decisions.note: Does not see it as an investable business to grow beyond its current state.
It is a secondary product that requires consumers to already own dumbbells.
Leverage his PRX gym deal and direct-to-consumer expertise to get into retail.
She can help them make more money and get preferred stock distributions.
Asks to lower the equity to 15%.
